title: Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones
summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Functional, CVSSv3.1: 7.5, CVEs: CVE-2026-113408, CVE-2026-114467, CVE-2026-114469, CVE-2026-105437, CVE-2026-114466, Summary: A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git. This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run. The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short. See also: https://lore.kernel.org/git/xmqqh5hosgw5.fsf@gitster.g/

title: VSA-2026-062: Empty-object login token
summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: High, CVSSv3.1: None, CVEs: , Summary: A vulnerability was discovered in Xen Orchestra that is part of the Xen Orchestra Appliance. We classify the impact as Critical. For details on how we assign severity levels, see our Severity Levels Explained page. This vulnerability is actively exploited by a threat actor operating intially from 91.211.251.112:8001 and ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333 (via Tor) REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs. Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2 (stable) and 6.10.1 (latest): Affected. Xen Orchestra Appliance: Affected. See also: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-xen-orchestra-auth-bypass-flaw-exploited-to-hijack-vm-servers/

REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. title: AI Harms Taxonomy
summary: Mapping the digital ways AI-enabled mechanisms can make consumers worse off, directly or indirectly. Plenty of people have made lists of the ways AI can go wrong. Very few of those lists tell you where different forces could get involved to stop the harms. So we built this around places to intervene. Each harm is traced through the points it passes on its way to the consumer, and each defense is attached at the point where it would actually have to be built. Doing it that way makes one thing very obvious: many of these harms are not ours to fix. They can only be fixed by the companies that make the models and run the products, and it seems better to say that than to pretend otherwise. Finally, this is a work in progress. Many entries list an evidence base, but some are still thin, and we are constantly reevaluating the structure of this taxonomy to keep pace with this fast-moving field. Your feedback is very welcome, especially if you think something is wrong.
summary_html:
Mapping the digital ways AI-enabled mechanisms can make consumers worse off, directly or indirectly.

Plenty of people have made lists of the ways AI can go wrong. Very few of those lists tell you where different forces could get involved to stop the harms.

So we built this around places to intervene. Each harm is traced through the points it passes on its way to the consumer, and each defense is attached at the point where it would actually have to be built.

Doing it that way makes one thing very obvious: many of these harms are not ours to fix. They can only be fixed by the companies that make the models and run the products, and it seems better to say that than to pretend otherwise.

Finally, this is a work in progress. Many entries list an evidence base, but some are still thin, and we are constantly reevaluating the structure of this taxonomy to keep pace with this fast-moving field. Your feedback is very welcome, especially if you think something is wrong.

title: SonicWall MFA Bypass Vulnerability Actively Exploited
summary: Classification: Important, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Proof-of-Concept, CVSSv3.1: 7.5, CVEs: CVE-2026-19868, Summary: Attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in the operating system that powers SonicWall firewalls to bypass multifactor authentication and gain access to the devices. The SSL VPN vulnerability enables attackers with valid credentials to bypass SAML - often used to facilitate single sign-on - as well as MFA, if it's tied to SAML, warns a security alert released Friday by SonicWall. The vulnerability in SonicWall Gen7 and Gen8 devices, assigned CVE-2026-19868, has a CVSS v3 score of 7.5. SonicOS versions up to and including 7.3.3-7015 and before, as well as 8.2.2-8015 and before, are vulnerable. SonicWall credited Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office, an IT services and consulting firm based in North Carolina, with discovering the flaw. Proof-of-concept code for exploiting CVE-2026-19868, in the form of a Python script, appeared Saturday on GitHub. "Needs working credentials for the alternate method," the tool's notes read. "Gives you an authenticated session that skipped SAML." The vulnerability can only be exploited if an administrator enables the SAML interface or service for the SSL VPN. Many organizations use SAML to facilitate easier logins for users, by letting them authenticate to an identity provider, or IdP, which then handles single sign-on between that user and multiple service providers, or SPs.

title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
summary: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

title: GhostFrame: A New ESXi Implant Linked to Settra Ransomware
summary: GhostFrame is a previously undocumented post-exploitation framework that gives threat actors extensive control over compromised VMware ESXi environments. Once an attacker gains root-level access to an ESXi host, GhostFrame provides a single interface to access virtual machines running on the hypervisor, harvest credentials, execute commands, and pivot deeper into victim networks. Insikt Group identified GhostFrame being used by TAG-218, a threat activity group whose operations overlap with Settra ransomware. GhostFrame is notable because it allows threat actors to operate from the virtualization layer, where a single compromised ESXi host can provide access to multiple virtual machines and the systems and data they contain. Insikt Group’s findings demonstrate how attackers can use compromised hypervisors as a centralized platform for post-exploitation activity, potentially expanding access across victim environments without compromising each virtual machine individually. The discovery highlights the importance of treating virtualization infrastructure as a high-value target and monitoring ESXi hosts for signs of unauthorized access and post-exploitation activity. Insikt Group identified GhostFrame, a command-and-control (C2) and post-exploitation framework designed to operate on compromised VMware ESXi hypervisors. GhostFrame provides threat actors with a centralized interface to maintain access to ESXi hosts, execute commands, manage virtual machines (VMs), pivot through internal networks, and harvest credentials from Windows systems hosted on the hypervisor. One notable feature is GhostFrame’s ability to operate from the virtualization layer. A single ESXi host can support multiple VMs running critical services within an organization. GhostFrame allows operators with root privileges on the hypervisor to interact with multiple hosted systems from a single point of access instead of requiring separate access to each guest system.

title: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier
summary: Mainstream software and malware can be reverse-engineered more easily than ever, thanks to artificial intelligence (AI) tools — something that security researchers are warning has implications for cyber defense, intellectual property (IP) theft, and beyond. Household applications typically run on hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lines of code. They incorporate hundreds of third-party libraries, gobs of files, and complex webs of interconnected components. Unpacking and mapping it all is exactly the kind of task that was so difficult before AI, but is now totally in range for even small teams and individuals. Cybersecurity researchers from Intezer recently tested out how easy it is to reverse-engineer software with AI by picking on some high-profile candidates: Slack, Apple's Finder app, and, importantly for security researchers, the Turla malware. Ironically, the malware proved the most difficult to wrangle. They found it only moderately challenging to meaningfully recreate Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps from the ground up. "It lowers the bar," Intezer senior security researcher and malware analyst Nicole Fishbein says of AI. "In the past, to reverse-engineer a software, you needed experience. You needed to understand Assembly, and it took a lot of time. Now, I don't want to say anyone [can do it], but it is much easier."

title: Exchange for breakfast: Turla’s Cereal tricks are not for kids
summary: On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user’s inbox. Somewhere in a national government office, an official sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, exactly as it should, and nothing looks suspicious. But before the email leaves the building, a piece of code quietly examines it, decides that it is interesting, and sets aside a copy to be forwarded to prying eyes, while the original email continues on its way. On November 28th, 2025, we found the toolset that installs such code on an Exchange server of a governmental organization in Kazakhstan. What initially looked like separate suspicious components soon revealed a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages. After fine-tuning our detections, we found the same toolset at a governmental organization in Romania – compromised on December 23rd, 2025 – where it was configured to identify emails sent to, or received from, The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and European Union (EU). One of the most interesting aspects of this toolset is what we did not find: external command and control (C&C) infrastructure. Instead – adding insult to injury – the victim’s compromised Exchange server is co-opted to act as the C&C infrastructure. We attribute Cereal, with high confidence, to the Russia-aligned APT group Turla, based on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware. The full technical analysis is available in our white paper.

title: Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Tracking CopperDragon’s Sparrow Framework Around the Globe
summary: Over the past year, Check Point Research investigated a series of intrusion campaigns targeting several dozens of high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. These campaigns initially appeared to be independent operations, each using different backdoors, post-exploitation tools and operational pace. However, we identified numerous connections between the tools and their infrastructure which linked them to the same Sparrow malware ecosystem. We track the entity behind these campaigns as CopperDragon, which may serve as a digital quartermaster supporting a number of China-nexus threat actors that use the Sparrow cross-platform malware framework for Linux and Windows. FamousSparrow is a threat actor that was first identified in 2021, whose main backdoor is SparrowDoor. Since then, multiple vendors have reported on related activity and malware variants, including CrowDoor, HemiGate, and TernDoor. Over time, it became apparent that this other activity was not necessarily carried out by the original FamousSparrow group. Instead, reporting pointed to several distinct actors using a shared toolset, potentially supplied by the same entity. These actors include FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, UAT-9244, and others. FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, but the relationship details remain unclear. Based on the apparent tool-sharing, we began tracking the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, its possible developer and supplier. In this report, we examine three distinct activity clusters targeting major telecommunications providers, government organizations, and military entities. Together, these operations provide a broader view of the connected and evolving espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon.

title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
summary: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness.

title: GhostShares 2: Grok Apps Exposed xAI’s Business Secrets and People’s Private Data
summary: We found more than 35,000 apps built with Grok that anyone with the link could open. Among them were SpaceXSI's own sales territory map, an X ad proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential, an ICU patient's lab results, a hospital group's staff list and a timesheet that hands out its employees' passwords. On November 8, 2026, we were working through a long list of web addresses under grok.me, the domain where Grok, the AI assistant from SpaceXSI (the company formerly called xAI), publishes the apps people build with it. Nobody had sent us any of them. We opened the first page of each one once, from the public internet and signed in to nothing, the way anyone would in an incognito window. One address named a new hire and ended in “onboarding plan”. It was the onboarding plan for a new member of SpaceXSI’s own enterprise sales team, marked confidential: the systems to get access to in the first week, internal system addresses, the sales team’s tools, 19 of the company’s internal chat channels, the colleagues to meet and a 30-day plan. Nothing asked us to sign in. We were shocked. The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. We call pages like this GhostShares: they open for people who were never given the link, and those people can find them on their own. Last month it was Meta’s Muse. This time it is the apps people make by describing them to Grok and publish from the same chat window.
summary_html:
We found more than 35,000 apps built with Grok that anyone with the link could open. Among them were SpaceXSI's own sales territory map, an X ad proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential, an ICU patient's lab results, a hospital group's staff list and a timesheet that hands out its employees' passwords.

On November 8, 2026, we were working through a long list of web addresses under grok.me, the domain where Grok, the AI assistant from SpaceXSI (the company formerly called xAI), publishes the apps people build with it. Nobody had sent us any of them. We opened the first page of each one once, from the public internet and signed in to nothing, the way anyone would in an incognito window.

One address named a new hire and ended in “onboarding plan”. It was the onboarding plan for a new member of SpaceXSI’s own enterprise sales team, marked confidential: the systems to get access to in the first week, internal system addresses, the sales team’s tools, 19 of the company’s internal chat channels, the colleagues to meet and a 30-day plan. Nothing asked us to sign in.

We were shocked. The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it.

We call pages like this GhostShares: they open for people who were never given the link, and those people can find them on their own. Last month it was Meta’s Muse. This time it is the apps people make by describing them to Grok and publish from the same chat window.

title: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon
summary: AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats. In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit. Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example. At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
summary: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate.

title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
summary: Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent. Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today. In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

title: Trusted by Default: Qubole Cross-Account Access Abused in the Wild
summary: Third-party integrations are one of the most common ways organizations grant outside parties access to their cloud environments. Working with Sentra and Mandiant, Wiz observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole between October 14 and October 26, 2026. The actor used these credentials to assume IAM roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account. Once inside multiple victim AWS environments, the threat actor enumerated resources, collected configuration and secrets, accessed S3 data, and validated additional credentials it discovered along the way. Sentra identified suspicious activity across several of their customer environments, recognized it as a broad supply chain attack, and shared the information with Wiz, prompting this investigation. This post describes what Wiz observed, how defenders can hunt for it, and how to reduce exposure from third-party cross-account trust relationships.

title: Hacking Two Automakers: ForgeRock Path Confusion, RCE, and Remote Vehicle Access
summary: In early 2026, Shubham Shah and I found a vulnerability chain that gave us remote code execution on the production ForgeRock servers handling customer logins for two automakers, which we'll call Automaker #1 and Automaker #2. From those servers, we could create a valid session for any customer account managed by the affected deployments. If the account had a connected vehicle, the session gave us the same remote access as the owner's app: its location and telemetry, door lock and unlock, and remote engine start and stop. After we reported the vulnerability, both automakers fixed it within about two hours and rotated the affected credentials. The affected systems served customers in multiple regions; we tested the complete chain only with US accounts and vehicles.

title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
summary: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote.

The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds.

One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel.

The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.”

Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible.

Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us.

“This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote.

title: Office Party: A Code-Execution Vulnerability in Anthropic's Official Office Skills Runs a Planted Binary
summary: Most skills are something you go looking for. Anthropic's docx, pptx and xlsx skills are already there. They are the skills behind Claude's own document features: when you ask Claude on claude.ai for a Word document, a slide deck or a spreadsheet, these skills are active with no setup, and Claude picks them on its own whenever a request calls for one. Anthropic also publishes them in its official anthropics/skills repository, describing them as "actively used in a production AI application", and Claude Code users install them from Anthropic's skills marketplace (anthropics/skills) as document-skills. In OpenAI Sesame, we showed that an official skill can be vulnerable on its own. This time the vulnerable skill is Anthropic's, and the vulnerability is a classic one: a trusted program that runs whatever file it finds in a shared folder. We call it Office Party: the file is an uninvited guest that crashes Anthropic's Office skills.

title: Pro-Russian hackers target European officials, offer rewards for personal information
summary: Pro-Russian hackers have published the personal information of Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and other senior European officials on the dark web, offering cryptocurrency rewards for additional details about them and their families. Tajani said Saturday the campaign was intended to intimidate him over Italy's support for Ukraine. "For days now, cybercriminals have been posting my personal data on the dark web and looking for more information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote Saturday on X. "They are also targeting my family." The campaign has been linked to NoName057(16), a pro-Russian hacktivist group best known for launching cyberattacks against Ukraine and European countries that support Kyiv. The group has published personal information about 18 European politicians, law enforcement officials and journalists on a dedicated dark web site, according to cybersecurity researchers who examined the material.

title: Portal breach at Germany's top university exposes every registered user's password
summary: Attackers stole central university login passwords belonging to everyone registered with the Technical University of Munich's myTUM portal, including an admin whose credentials were then used to attack a second system. TUM restored access to its TUMonline campus management system on Monday morning, allowing users to change their passwords. The university disclosed the attack on November 6. The initial attack targeted the myTUM portal, which serves students and faculty members, providing centralized online access to services and documents. TUM said the attackers used the admin's credentials to launch a follow-on attack on TUMonline, its central campus management system, which forced the IT team to take it offline. The university has not disclosed how the attackers initially gained access or how the stolen passwords were stored. It did not immediately answer questions about the number of affected users.

title: Ukraine dismantles crypto scam network that stole €4.3 million
summary: Ukrainian law enforcement arrested four suspects in a case involving the theft of more than €4.3 million using a network of cryptocurrency investment scam call centers. In these fraud schemes (also known as romance baiting or pig butchering scams), criminals lure targets through social media, dating sites, and messaging apps into fake investment schemes, stealing their money instead of investing the funds as promised. The investigation involved Ukraine's Cyber Police Department, the Main Investigation Department of the National Police of Ukraine, and German law enforcement authorities. According to Ukraine's Cyber Police, the suspects used phone calls and messaging apps to build victims' trust through social engineering and trick them into investing in cryptocurrency, shares, and other financial instruments through fraudulent online trading platforms. The crime ring targeted potential victims across the European Union, stealing more than €4.3 million from 135 German victims.

title: N-able Takes Platform Offline After 33 Zero-Days Drop
summary: A major security situation is unfolding for N-able and its customers, after a researcher on Monday dropped 33 zero-day vulnerabilities at once for the vendor's software. N-able declared an "active incident" Monday at 15:15 UTC, noting that it's experiencing a "major outage" of its hosted N-central services as it responds "to a public disclosure and non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central found by an independent researcher." The Burlington, Massachusetts-based company said that "as a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation." The company strongly urged all customers using on-premises versions of its N-central platform to likewise "temporarily take their N-central servers offline until further notice from N-able." N-able's N-central remote monitoring and management and unified endpoint management platform is widely used by managed security providers to administer customers' computers.
summary_html:
A major security situation is unfolding for N-able and its customers, after a researcher on Monday dropped 33 zero-day vulnerabilities at once for the vendor's software.

N-able declared an "active incident" Monday at 15:15 UTC, noting that it's experiencing a "major outage" of its hosted N-central services as it responds "to a public disclosure and non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central found by an independent researcher."

The Burlington, Massachusetts-based company said that "as a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation."

The company strongly urged all customers using on-premises versions of its N-central platform to likewise "temporarily take their N-central servers offline until further notice from N-able."

N-able's N-central remote monitoring and management and unified endpoint management platform is widely used by managed security providers to administer customers' computers.

title: France blames Iran for fridge cyberattacks, says some caused fires
summary: French authorities on Monday accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of a cyberattack sabotaging refrigeration systems at around 700 French grocery stores last month, causing what it said were extensive food losses and at least 15 fires. The accusation was made in a five-page report published Monday by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre, which brings together the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI, the military’s cyber command and the DGSE and DGSI intelligence services. In the first attribution since the October attacks, the French authorities identified the perpetrators as part of Shahid Kaveh, an IRGC cyber unit previously linked to attacks on industrial controllers at U.S. water utilities. France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters at a G7 ministerial meeting in Paris that he could confirm the IRGC was responsible for the fridge attacks, describing the sabotage as unprecedented in its scale and aggressiveness. France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and Barrot said the country will pursue European sanctions against those responsible.

title: Amadeuksen globaalissa tietovuodossa on ollut mukana myös Finnairin asiakkaiden tietoja
summary: Finnair on saanut tiedon globaalilta matkailualan järjestelmätoimittajalta Amadeukselta Amadeuksen varaustietoihin kohdistuneesta tietovuodosta. Amadeus tarjoaa varaus- ja lipunmyyntiohjelmistoja lentoyhtiöille, hotelleille ja matkatoimistoille ympäri maailmaa. Finnairin Amadeukselta saaman tiedon mukaan tietovuodon kohteena ovat useiden lentoyhtiöiden matkustajalistat. Näihin sisältyy yhteensä noin 116 000 Finnairin varausta. Näistä noin 750 varausta on Amadeuksen mukaan avattu tarkastelua varten ja näistä noin 30 varausta liittyy Aurinkomatkojen valmismatkoihin. Amadeuksen mukaan luvaton toiminta on pysäytetty. Vain murto-osa tarkastelluista varauksista on enää aktiivisia, ja nämä varaukset Finnair on vaihtanut uusille varausnumeroille. ”Olemme vaatineet Amadeukselta perusteellista selvitystä tapahtuneesta”, sanoo Finnairin tietoturvajohtaja Timo Arndal. ”Yksityiskohtainen selvitystyö on vielä kesken. Olemme kuitenkin saaneet Amadeukselta vahvistuksen siitä, että luottokorttitietoja tai salasanoja ei ole vaarantunut. Finnairin järjestelmiin ei ole tunkeuduttu.”

Kansainvälinen televiestintäliitto linjaa digitaaliteknologioiden globaalista kehityssuunnasta
summary: 9.11.2026 Tiedotteet Kansainvälinen televiestintäliitto linjaa digitaaliteknologioiden globaalista kehityssuunnasta Suomi osallistuu Kansainvälisen televiestintäliiton (ITU) täysivaltaisten edustajien konferenssiin, joka järjestetään Dohassa, Qatarissa 9.-27.11.2026. Suomi edistää kokouksessa globaalia 6G-järjestelmää sekä uusien satelliitti- ja tekoälyratkaisujen huomioimista tieto- ja viestintäteknologioiden kehityksessä. ITU:n yleiskokous yleiskokous Qatarissa Dohassa (Kuva: ITU/M. Faeas) Kansainvälisen televiestintäliiton (eng. International Telecommunications Union, lyhenne ITU) täysivaltaisten edustajien konferenssi eli yleiskokous kokoontuu Qatarissa Dohassa 9.-27.11.2026. ITU on YK:n tieto- ja viestintäteknologioiden erityisjärjestö ja keskeinen toimija digitaaliteknologioiden kehityksessä globaalisti. Sen tehtävänä on edistää maailmanlaajuisia digitaalisia yhteyksiä sopimalla radiotaajuuksien käytöstä ja yhteisistä standardeista ja sekä edistämällä digitaalisten palvelujen saatavuutta. Vuoden 2026 yleiskokouksessa keskeisiksi temaattisiksi painopisteiksi ovat nousemassa tekoäly osana televiestintäsektorin kehitystä, digitaalisen infrastruktuurin turvallisuus ja häiriönsietokyky sekä uudet satelliittiteknologiat. Teknologioiden geopoliittisen merkityksen kasvaessa kansainvälisten standardien, radiotaajuuksien ja digitaalisen infrastruktuurin kehittämiseen liittyvillä päätöksillä on entistä laajempia taloudellisia ja turvallisuuspoliittisia vaikutuksia. Suomen tavoitteena ITU:ssa on varmistaa kestävät, turvalliset ja maailmanlaajuisesti toimivat tietoliikenneyhteydet ja suomalaisten yritysten kilpailukyky. Suomen keskeinen tavoite yleiskokouksessa on seuraavan sukupolven matkaviestinteknologioiden eli 6G:n edistäminen. Suomi pitää tärkeänä, että ITU edistää globaalin 6G-järjestelmän kehittämistä ja sen turvallista käyttöönottoa digitaalisia kuiluja kaventaen. Suomi on yhdessä toimialan teollisuuden ja kumppanimaiden kanssa valmistellut päätöslauselmaesityksen edistämään uusien laajakaistateknologioiden, erityisesti 6G:n, kehitystä ja käyttöönottoa. 6G-, tekoäly- ja satelliittiteemojen lisäksi Suomi vaikuttaa aktiivi-sesti muun muassa älykaupunkeja, merikaapelien häiriönsietokykyä ja haitallisten radiotaajuushäiriöiden torjuntaa koskevissa neuvotteluissa. Koska Venäjältä kantautuvaa satelliittinavigoinnin (GNSS) ja matkaviestinverkkojen häirintää havaitaan jatkuvasti Suomen ja Itämeren alueella, Suomi tuo yhdessä samanmielisten maiden kanssa yleiskokouksen käsiteltäväksi päätöslauselmaesityksen haitallisiin radiohäiriöihin puuttumiseksi. Suomi osallistuu konferenssiin valtuuskunnalla, jonka puheenjohtajana toimii ylijohtaja Laura Eiro liikenne- ja viestintäministeriöstä. Kansainvälinen televiestintäliitto linjaa digitaaliteknologioiden globaalista kehityssuunnasta

Suomi osallistuu Kansainvälisen televiestintäliiton (ITU) täysivaltaisten edustajien konferenssiin, joka järjestetään Dohassa, Qatarissa 9.-27.11.2026. Suomi edistää kokouksessa globaalia 6G-järjestelmää sekä uusien satelliitti- ja tekoälyratkaisujen huomioimista tieto- ja viestintäteknologioiden kehityksessä.

ITU:n yleiskokous yleiskokous Qatarissa Dohassa (Kuva: ITU/M. Faeas)

Kansainvälisen televiestintäliiton (eng. International Telecommunications Union, lyhenne ITU) täysivaltaisten edustajien konferenssi eli yleiskokous kokoontuu Qatarissa Dohassa 9.-27.11.2026. ITU on YK:n tieto- ja viestintäteknologioiden erityisjärjestö ja keskeinen toimija digitaaliteknologioiden kehityksessä globaalisti. Sen tehtävänä on edistää maailmanlaajuisia digitaalisia yhteyksiä sopimalla radiotaajuuksien käytöstä ja yhteisistä standardeista ja sekä edistämällä digitaalisten palvelujen saatavuutta.

Vuoden 2026 yleiskokouksessa keskeisiksi temaattisiksi painopisteiksi ovat nousemassa tekoäly osana televiestintäsektorin kehitystä, digitaalisen infrastruktuurin turvallisuus ja häiriönsietokyky sekä uudet satelliittiteknologiat. Teknologioiden geopoliittisen merkityksen kasvaessa kansainvälisten standardien, radiotaajuuksien ja digitaalisen infrastruktuurin kehittämiseen liittyvillä päätöksillä on entistä laajempia taloudellisia ja turvallisuuspoliittisia vaikutuksia. 

Suomen tavoitteena ITU:ssa on varmistaa kestävät, turvalliset ja maailmanlaajuisesti toimivat tietoliikenneyhteydet ja suomalaisten yritysten kilpailukyky. Suomen keskeinen tavoite yleiskokouksessa on seuraavan sukupolven matkaviestinteknologioiden eli 6G:n edistäminen. Suomi pitää tärkeänä, että ITU edistää globaalin 6G-järjestelmän kehittämistä ja sen turvallista käyttöönottoa digitaalisia kuiluja kaventaen. Suomi on yhdessä toimialan teollisuuden ja kumppanimaiden kanssa valmistellut päätöslauselmaesityksen edistämään uusien laajakaistateknologioiden, erityisesti 6G:n, kehitystä ja käyttöönottoa.  

6G-, tekoäly- ja satelliittiteemojen lisäksi Suomi vaikuttaa aktiivi-sesti muun muassa älykaupunkeja, merikaapelien häiriönsietokykyä ja haitallisten radiotaajuushäiriöiden torjuntaa koskevissa neuvotteluissa. Koska Venäjältä kantautuvaa satelliittinavigoinnin (GNSS) ja matkaviestinverkkojen häirintää havaitaan jatkuvasti Suomen ja Itämeren alueella, Suomi tuo yhdessä samanmielisten maiden kanssa yleiskokouksen käsiteltäväksi päätöslauselmaesityksen haitallisiin radiohäiriöihin puuttumiseksi. 

Suomi osallistuu konferenssiin valtuuskunnalla, jonka puheenjohtajana toimii ylijohtaja Laura Eiro liikenne- ja viestintäministeriöstä. Valtuuskuntaan kuuluu jäseniä liikenne- ja viestintäministeriöstä, ulkoministeriöstä ja Liikenne- ja viestintävirasto Traficomista. Suomen valtuuskunnassa on lisäksi mukana asiantuntijoina Nokia Oyj:n edustajia.  

Täysivaltaisten edustajien konferenssi kokoontuu joka neljäs vuosi. Konferenssissa hyväksytään järjestön teknistä työtä ohjaavat päätöslauselmat sekä järjestön nelivuotinen strateginen ja taloudellinen suunnitelma. Lisäksi konferenssissa valitaan järjestön ylin johto ja hallintoneuvoston jäsenvaltiot. ITU:n päätöksillä on merkittävä vaikutus kansalliseen päätöksentekoon ja telealan markkinoiden kehitykseen, etenkin radiotaajuuksien ja kansainvälisten teknisten standardien osalta.

title: Ministeri Tavio edistää suomalaisia puhtaan energian kaupallisia ratkaisuja YK:n ilmastokokouksessa Antalyassa
summary: 9.11.2026 Tiedotteet Ministeri Tavio edistää suomalaisia puhtaan energian kaupallisia ratkaisuja YK:n ilmastokokouksessa Antalyassa Ulkomaankauppa- ja kehitysministeri Ville Tavio matkustaa Antalyaan, Turkkiin 10.–12. marraskuuta. Ministeri Tavio osallistuu YK:n ilmastosopimusten osapuolikokouksen (COP31) yhteydessä järjestettäviin tapahtumiin ja avaa Suomen paviljongin. Ohjelmassa on myös kahdenvälisiä tapaamisia ja keskusteluja elinkeinoelämän edustajien kanssa. YK:n 31. ilmastosopimusten osapuolikokous kokoaa jopa 100 000 osallistujaa ympäri maailmaa neuvottelemaan ilmastotoimien edistämisestä sekä keskustelemaan puhtaan siirtymän tarjoamista taloudellisista mahdollisuuksista. Kokous tarjoaa Suomelle keskeisen foorumin käydä vuoropuhelua kansainvälisten kumppaneiden kanssa ja vahvistaa Suomen asemaa ratkaisukeskeisenä ilmastotoimijana. ”Suomen hallitus tukee puhdasta siirtymää ja haluamme tuoda esille suomalaista osaamista ja teknologisia ratkaisuja, jotka tuovat myös talouskasvua ja parantavat kilpailukykyä”, ministeri Tavio toteaa. Kyseessä on kolmas kerta, kun Suomella on oma paviljonki YK:n ilmastokokouksessa. Paviljonki toteutetaan laajassa yhteistyössä suomalaisen elinkeinoelämän, korkeakoulujen, tutkimuslaitosten, kaupunkien ja kansalaisyhteiskunnan kanssa. Mukana ovat muun muassa hankkeen käynnistäneet Climate Leadership Coalition, Elinkeinoelämän keskusliitto, Keskuskauppakamari, Teknologiateollisuus ry ja UN Global Compact Suomi, sekä paviljongin pääyhteistyökumppanit Outokumpu ja Neste. Ministeri avaa Suomen paviljongin 10. marraskuuta ja osallistuu tilaisuuksiin, joissa käsitellään muun muassa puhtaan energian, sähköistymisen ja digitalisaation merkitystä ilmastotoimille, talouskasvulle ja kilpailukyvylle. Lisäksi ministeri osallistuu Nuorten Agenda2030 -ryhmän paneeliin, jossa pohditaan, miten ilmastotavoitteet saadaan muutettua käytännön toimiksi yritysten ja päättäjien yhteistyöllä. ”Suomen paviljonki Antalyassa osoittaa, että haluamme rakentaa ilmastoratkaisuja yhdessä. Suomalaisyrityksillä on tarjota teknologioita, osaamista ja investointeja, jotka tukevat puhdasta energiasiirtymää, kiertotaloutta ja teollisuuden päästövähennyksiä”, ministeri Tavio korostaa. Ministerin ohjelmaan sisältyy lisäksi kahdenvälisiä tapaamisia sekä keskusteluja elinkeinoelämän edustajien kanssa. Suomen valtuuskuntaa kokouksessa johtaa tasavallan presidentti Alexander Stubb . Lisäksi kokoukseen osallistuvat ympäristöministeri Sari Multala sekä elinkeinoministeri Sakari Puisto . Lisätietoja: Laura Lindgren, yksikönpäällikkö, ulkoministeriön ilmasto- ja ympäristödiplomatian yksikkö, puh. +358 295 350 024 Soili Kangaskorpi, ilmasto- ja ympäristösuurlähettiläs, ulkoministeriön ilmasto- ja ympäristödiplomatian yksikkö, puh. +358 295 350 008 Timo Sysiö, diplomaattiavustaja, ulkomaankauppa- ja kehitysministerin kabinetti, puh. +358 503134917 Ulkoministeriön sähköpostiosoitteet ovat muotoa etunimi.sukunimi@gov.fi Suomen paviljongin ohjelma Antalyan ilmastokokouksen verkkosivu (englanniksi)

title: Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast
summary: The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain. On the night of Oct. 11, an unknown attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process. The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems. What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

title: Microsoft Paint RCE Fix Now Available, but Windows Update Won't Deliver It
summary: A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates. The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today. The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13. Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix. His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear.

title: The Port That Does Not Exist
summary: Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193...or 58037...or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you. But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner's default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn't a real port. Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings.

title: FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.4 million in crypto from nation-state hackers
summary: A senior FBI official pleaded guilty to stealing millions in cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by nation-state hackers and theft victims. Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts. Yaroch was an FBI Supervisory Special Agent who worked at FBI Headquarters within the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division — with his work focusing on an unnamed nation-state. He used his seniority to access FBI systems that had the codes and passwords necessary to take cryptocurrency from at least two adversarial nations as well as 10 victims of crimes. In total, he conducted 100 transfers from 79 wallets starting in December 2024. The wallets were connected to 35 different FBI investigations.

title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
summary: D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches. These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments. While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets. Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.

title: QNAP says hackers breaching NAS devices in Plex2Shell attacks
summary: QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version available in the QNAP App Center, as hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain. The vendor said it had received multiple reports of suspected compromises involving customers’ network-attached storage (NAS) devices. "QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through [Plex2Shell] vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected users,” the company says in an advisory today.

title: UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes
summary: The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments. The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency. But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year. Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams. But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access for the two models for several weeks.

title: Runaway AI hacking agent behind WorkOS breach after escaping sandbox
summary: WorkOS says an AI-powered hacking agent that breached its internal sales application and accessed customer information was operated by a security researcher who claims the tool escaped its testing environment and unintentionally attacked the company. The developer platform disclosed the breach earlier this week, saying an attacker used the ARTEX AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts against its systems. However, in a new security update published Friday, WorkOS founder Michael Grinich revealed that the person responsible had come forward and claimed the incident was accidental. "Shortly after our original bulletin, a security researcher contacted us and claimed responsibility," Grinich said in a post on X. "They told us they were evaluating ARTEX, an autonomous penetration testing framework, when their agent escaped its isolated testing environment and interacted with WorkOS unintentionally.”

title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization. Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

title: Agents reveal secrets when offered to team up with each other
summary: AI agents will break security rules, revealing their secrets to strangers, and running untrusted code in exchange for help from a swarm of other agents, according to test results shared with The Register. The test - part of an internal hackathon sponsored by the nonprofit AI Alignment Foundation and run by AE Studio - asked nine AI coding agents to fix a bug: a broken pricing service. The testers also gave the agents a private token, told them to keep it private, and gave them access to a forum of 24 other agents. The forum held the fix, and the swarm asked the nine to share their secret token and run an install script before they would help them fix the bug. Across 181 trials with that swarm, agents posted the token 15 percent of the time and ran the script 24 percent of the time, compared to 2 percent and 0 percent on an ordinary help forum.

title: SonicWall SonicOS Affected By Multiple Vulnerabilities
summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 8.8, CVEs: CVE-2026-77708, CVE-2026-77709, CVE-2026-82308, CVE-2026-107154, CVE-2026-107155, CVE-2026-19703, CVE-2026-19868, Summary: SonicWall has released security updates to fix seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868, allows attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls, potentially including SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA). The flaw has a CVSS severity score of 7.1 and only affects SonicOS SSL-VPN services configured to use SAML authentication. The advisory also fixes six additional vulnerabilities in SonicOS, including two management interface flaws rated 8.8 severity that allow unauthenticated attackers to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions. The advisory also fixes six additional vulnerabilities in SonicOS, including two management interface flaws rated 8.8 severity that allow unauthenticated attackers to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions. See also: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-new-ssl-vpn-mfa-bypass-flaw-exploited-in-attacks/

title: Coding Agents Copy Your Secrets to a Hidden File. Thousands Are on GitHub
summary: Apiiro research found 2,539 real secrets in 1,994 public GitHub repositories: database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, SSH root logins. Among them: a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database. 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes, are affected. One confirmed its key had been live. Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file. It asks before running it. Pick "Yes, and don't ask again" and it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder. Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code. Out of 104,185 public copies of this file on GitHub, 1,122 hold a real secret. We found 1,160 more in git history, in the shared settings.json teams commit on purpose, and in agent chat transcripts saved in repos. GitHub is just where we could count. The same file sits in plain text on every laptop where someone clicked "don't ask again." Malware already collects credentials from developer machines in bulk.

title: Hackers pull off $133 million French bank heist via service provider
summary: French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was targeted in a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions of up to $133 million, forcing it to respond by suspending certain systems. The bank says that the attacker used its own account to initiate transactions to other banking organizations, but customer assets remain unaffected. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa is a major French banking group with more than 5.8 million members and 211.5 billion euros in assets. Reports about the incident emerged on November 2, initially from blockchain fraud investigator ZachXBT, who warned of a large-scale unauthorized withdrawal from multiple centralized exchange accounts occurring a day earlier. According to the investigator, the attacker may have stolen up to 118 million euros ($133 million) and withdrawn it as USDC and USDT stablecoins.

title: Barracuda Networks is your new best friend (Barracuda Email Security Gateway Pre-Auth Remote Root RCE CVE-2026-116606 / CVE-2026-111560)
summary: What Is A Barracuda, And Why? Must We? Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway solution (ESG) is no stranger to love, for a couple of reasons: For many, it is the appliance that sits in front of an organization's mail and decides which messages are spam, which carry malware, and which are allowed through. For others, it’s the appliance that required physical replacement after UNC4841 (per Mandiant) exploited CVE-2023-2868 as a zero-day. Whoever you are, one thing will be consistent in your experience: it is yet another appliance that lives at the edge, inspects everything, and runs with the exact and only privileges needed to block a mean email about your blog post.

title: DoJ's 'Super Intelligence Task Force' up and running
summary: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) says its Super Intelligence Task Force (SINTF) is now up and running, after president Donald Trump ordered the move in a memo last month. Headed up by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as associate attorney general Stanley Woodward and associate deputy attorney general Stephen Weiss, SINTF's responsibility is to protect the US's lead in artificial intelligence development. Thursday's announcement, which was littered with the "super intelligence" Trumpism, said the task force will ensure the US's SI/AI leadership remains uncompromised by foreign AI "abuse," including by state and state-backed groups, criminal enterprises, individuals, or corporate entities.

title: US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos
summary: Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more. In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more. Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

title: White House IP Addresses Sold Through Proxy Services
summary: Devices on the White House network are being used as proxies allowing outside users to appear as if they come from the president's office, researchers found. Security firm Layer3 Intel stumbled on the White House network while probing services that sell access to everyday devices for traffic reroute. It found that 28 residential proxy services provided access to the Washington network. Between Oct. 5 and Nov. 3, those providers routed researchers' internet traffic through six White House IP addresses hundreds of times. "We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it," Layer3 Intel said Wednesday in a blog. "We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services." Traffic from the White House devices showed up between 5 p.m. and midnight and almost none in the early morning. The pattern suggests that it came from a person powering on the devices and regularly working late rather than a public guest Wi-Fi, Layer3 Intel said.

title: DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information
summary: DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents. The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed. In an email seen by The Register, DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents. DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing.

title: Vulnerability in Rapid7 Metasploit
summary: Classification: Important, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv4.0: 7.3, CVEs: CVE-2026-121139, Summary: The Rapid7 Metasploit msf-ws suffers from a missing authentication vulnerability whereby the REST API grants an unauthenticated "bootstrap" exemption so that the very first administrator can be created when the users table is empty. While the table is empty, POST /api/v1/users is exempt from authentication by design: the route handler calls warden.authenticate!(scope: :admin_api), which resolves to AdminApiToken. The inherited ApiToken#authenticate! short-circuits and returns success!() whenever msf.auth_initialized is false, without ever evaluating AdminApiToken's administrator check. In that state the endpoint creates a user — including an administrator — for an entirely unauthenticated caller. See also: https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/pull/22039

title: Harden cooling systems now, feds warn critical infrastructure operators amid attacks
summary: The warning, issued by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI and others, comes after hundreds of supermarkets across Europe had their refrigerators remotely hacked and temperatures raised, resulting in potentially millions of euros of spoiled food. Earlier this week, cooling unit controls were tampered with at three of France’s national blood banks, the French Blood Establishment announced, though it’s unclear if the incidents are linked. In their advisory, federal agencies noted that organizations in the healthcare, transportation, food and chemicals sectors “widely” use cooling systems that rely on “automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.” They cautioned that malicious actors may exploit vulnerabilities in “unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

title: Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns
summary: Key Points - Agentic hacking platforms like ARTEX, where AI models autonomously drive vulnerability discovery and exploitation, have been observed to be used by various cyber criminals. - Check Point Research’s analysis of the current landscape observed more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX alone, showing a massive scale of deployments. - While previous threat reports on ARTEX focused on the observed telemetry on the victim side, we present artifacts from the operator consoles. This data shows which models were used as well as how the operators prompted their agents. - Most attacks were fully autonomous besides the initial goal setup. Threat actors barely interacted with their agent fleets. - In the observed activity, Chinese models are most prevalent, with Deepseek Flash taking the lead. - Operators mostly only interacted with their agents to check the progress of the current operations – attacks were almost fully autonomous. - The goals set by the attackers were exclusively to carry out opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. Agents abused various web vulnerabilities, such as Remote Code Execution (RCE), to achieve their goals. In some cases, agents were using the access gained to actively carry out supply chain attacks.
summary_html:
Key Points

- Agentic hacking platforms like ARTEX, where AI models autonomously drive vulnerability discovery and exploitation, have been observed to be used by various cyber criminals.

- Check Point Research’s analysis of the current landscape observed more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX alone, showing a massive scale of deployments.

- While previous threat reports on ARTEX focused on the observed telemetry on the victim side, we present artifacts from the operator consoles. This data shows which models were used as well as how the operators prompted their agents.

- Most attacks were fully autonomous besides the initial goal setup. Threat actors barely interacted with their agent fleets.

- In the observed activity, Chinese models are most prevalent, with Deepseek Flash taking the lead. 

- Operators mostly only interacted with their agents to check the progress of the current operations – attacks were almost fully autonomous.

- The goals set by the attackers were exclusively to carry out opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. Agents abused various web vulnerabilities, such as Remote Code Execution (RCE), to achieve their goals. In some cases, agents were using the access gained to actively carry out supply chain attacks.

title: Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
summary: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues.

title: Chainalysis warns all users hit in cyber breach involving ‘agentic’ techniques
summary: Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics company, said Wednesday night that some information belonging to all its users — which its website says include those in the law enforcement and national security sectors — had been exposed in a cyberattack. The company initially disclosed a breach on October 30, although at the time said it had found no evidence that authentication credentials or session tokens had been accessed. In its latest update, posted Wednesday night, the company said it had discovered “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.” The perpetrator was not identified. Chainalysis previously said it had “detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.” It has not explained what it meant by “offensive agentic techniques.” The company initially told customers the breach came amid what it described as “an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks.” Although it initially mentioned agentic techniques, it did not explicitly say its own breach was caused by an AI agent.

title: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
summary: Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long. OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16. The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default. The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.

Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.

The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.

title: Vulnerabilities in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10
summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 8.2, CVEs: CVE-2026-121994, CVE-2026-121995, CVE-2026-121996, CVE-2026-121997, Summary: CVE-2026-121994 (CVSS: 8.8): A stack buffer overflow in the GDB client's remote protocol handler allows an attacker-controlled debug target to execute arbitrary code in the GDB process. The vulnerability exists in fetch_register_using_p, which decodes a stub's register reply into an alloca-sized buffer without bounding writes by the register width. CVE-2026-121995 (CVSS: 7.5): A stack buffer overflow in the GDB client's tracepoint upload handler allows an attacker-controlled debug stub to corrupt stack memory automatically during connection setup. The overflow results from GDB reading beyond the current reply boundary into a stale prior reply in the shared packet buffer. CVE-2026-121996 (CVSS: 8.2): A length validation flaw in gdbserver's agent-expression parser allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to read uninitialized heap memory from the gdbserver process and cause a denial of service. Disclosed heap content includes addresses suitable for defeating ASLR in further exploitation. CVE-2026-121997 (CVSS: 8.1): A heap buffer overflow in gdbserver's QTDPsrc packet handler allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve native code execution in the gdbserver process. The vulnerability results from a mismatch between a packet's declared source length and the actual data length, causing hex2bin to write beyond the allocated heap buffer. title: Zyxel GS1900 Patch Fails to Block Zero-Day Exploit Allowing Root Command Execution
summary: Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found. The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole. The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week. The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then. GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found.
